common_name: Ego Siberian Iris (Pale Blue-Violet Ruffled Iris)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Ego was bred by Currier McEwen and is the parent of the later, deeper-toned 'Super Ego'.

directions: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Ego carries soft pale blue-violet standards and falls with a ruffled edge and a small white signal patch, a gentler counterpart to the deeper-colored Siberian iris cultivars later bred from it. Like other Siberian iris, it tolerates wetter soil than bearded iris and rarely suffers from rot or borer problems, making it a dependable, low-fuss choice for a mixed border or pond margin. Clumps can remain undisturbed for many years and only need dividing once flowering declines in a crowded center.

common_name: Tropic Night Siberian Iris (Near-Black Deep Violet Self)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Tropic Night is prized as one of the darkest, near-black-purple Siberian iris cultivars widely available.

directions: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Tropic Night opens extremely dark, near-black violet-purple flowers with a velvety sheen, a dramatic contrast plant for pairing next to pale or white perennials in a border or pond-edge planting. Foliage forms narrow, grass-like clumps that stay tidy well after bloom finishes, and the plant shares the Siberian iris group's general resistance to the rot and borer problems that trouble bearded iris. Established clumps can go many years without division, needing it only once the center thins out and bloom count drops.

common_name: Cambridge Siberian Iris (White with Sky-Blue Edge)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Cambridge is an older Cassebeer-bred cultivar valued for its crisp white-and-blue bitone pattern.

directions: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Cambridge bears mostly white flowers whose falls carry a rim of clear sky blue, giving the clump a crisp bitone look distinct from the many solid-blue or solid-violet Siberian iris cultivars. Narrow, grass-like foliage stays attractive as a textural accent through summer once bloom finishes, and the plant tolerates wetter soil and shrugs off the rot and borer problems that plague bearded iris. Divide only when the clump becomes crowded and flowering starts to decline, ideally in early fall or right after spring bloom.

common_name: Freckled Peacock Japanese Iris (White Speckled with Blue-Violet)

planting.note: Plant divisions in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to light partial shade; Freckled Peacock was bred by Marty Schafer and Jan Sacks of Joe Pye Weed's Garden and is known for its heavily speckled petal pattern.

directions: Plant divisions in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun to light partial shade. Freckled Peacock displays a white ground heavily peppered and speckled with blue-violet dots and flecks, a distinctive stippled pattern that sets it apart from the solid-colored or simply veined Japanese iris cultivars more commonly grown. As with other Japanese iris, it needs steadily moist, acidic soil through the growing season and sulks or declines quickly if the bed dries out, though it should not sit in standing water year-round. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years in early fall to keep plants vigorous and floriferous.
